Ramsay dates the Seleucid re-foundation of Tarsus as a Greek city-state (Antioch-on-the-Cydnus) by Antiochus IV Epiphanes to 171-170 BCE and argues that the new citizens then introduced included a body of Jews enrolled as a separate citizen Tribe; 'the Jews of Tarsus were, as a body, citizens with full burgess rights'. He infers a 'considerable body of Jews in Tarsus' from Acts and a 'strong body of Jews' from Epiphanius (Panarion 30, 4th c. CE, outside period). No count. Caveat: this is Ramsay's inference from Seleucid colonial practice and Paul's citizenship, not a direct ancient attestation; 2 Macc 4:30 (revolt of Tarsus and Mallus c. 171 BCE) does not mention Jews. Ramsay, 'Tarsus', The Expositor 7th series vol. 2 (1906), ch. XI (PDF text extracted locally).

A. Souter, 'Tarsus', Hastings' Dictionary of the Bible: Antiochus Epiphanes re-founded Tarsus as an autonomous city c. 171-170 BCE (cf. 2 Macc 4:30); 'a large body of Jews also was added to the population by Antiochus', incorporated 'as citizens in a new tribe by themselves'; 'the majority must have been citizens with full burghers' rights'; St Paul and probably his 'kinsmen' (Rom 16) were citizens of Tarsus enrolled in the Jewish tribe. Presence of a sizeable Jewish citizen body asserted ('a large body') but no number; presented as almost certain by the author, i.e. a scholarly inference. Year = midpoint of 171-170 BCE (c.).

Jewish Encyclopedia (1906), 'Tarsus': Jews 'had been colonized at Tarsus by the Seleucids about 170 B.C.' and were affected by the city's Hellenization; under Antiochus Epiphanes 'a revolt of these colonists' is linked to 2 Macc 4:30-38 (note: the biblical text speaks of 'the people of Tarsus and of Mallus' and does not name Jews). Cites Ramsay (followed by Schürer) that Jews could be citizens of a Greek town only if the sovereign organised them as a separate body, probably under Antiochus Epiphanes. Later evidence it cites (R. Nahum b. Simai preaching at Tarsus; Jaffa epitaph of Judah b. Joseph of Tarsus; 'Isaac, elder of the synagogue of the Cappadocians at Tarsus'; Rome epitaph of Asaphat of Tarsus) is post-70 CE and outside this period. c. 170 BCE; no count.

Encyclopedia of the Bible (Bible Gateway), 'Tarsus': in 171 BCE Antiochus Epiphanes conceded wider autonomy to Tarsus, one provision being 'a "tribe" of Jews with full citizenship'; 'Pompey no doubt found in the Tarsian Jews a force making for tranquility and order' and Roman citizenship was 'prob.' conferred on a group of Jews at Tarsus in this period (Pompey's eastern settlement; source dates his command to 63 BCE, c.). Describes 'Tarsian Jewry, proud of their city, willingly integrated into its social system'. Interpretive scholarly statement of an established Jewish community; no count. The same page's figure of 'half a million' for Tarsus is a total-city estimate (undated, mixed gentile city) and is NOT used as Jewish population.

Birth of Paul (Saul) of Tarsus, c. 5 CE (the article says likely between 5 BCE and 5 CE), in Tarsus, Cilicia, to 'a devout Jewish family' (Pharisees, tribe of Benjamin); implies a resident Jewish family, likely Roman citizens, in Tarsus around the turn of the era. Individual-level presence; no count. Wikipedia used as last resort for the date; the birth in Tarsus itself is Acts 22:3.

Mark Wilson, 'Cilicia: The First Christian Churches in Anatolia', Tyndale Bulletin 54.1 (2003): after his conversion Paul was sent from Jerusalem/Caesarea back to his home city Tarsus (Acts 9:30; Gal 1:21); first Jerusalem visit dated AD 32-33 (Ramsay) or AD 37 (Jewett) - year c. 37 per Jewett. Wilson holds Paul's family were Diaspora Jews living in Tarsus, possibly settled there by Antiochus IV (who 'settled Jews in Cilicia in 171 BC', after Ramsay) and receiving Roman citizenship in the mid-1st c. BCE (conjecture); notes Wallace & Williams (1998) consider a formative Tarsian context for Paul 'built on insecure foundations'. Paul's synagogue lashings (2 Cor 11:24) may belong to this Cilician phase, implying a synagogue in Tarsus. No count.

Wilson (Tyndale Bulletin 54.1, 2003) quoting Hengel & Schwemer (Paul Between Damascus and Antioch, 1997, p. 161): epigraphic evidence for Jews in Tarsus and Cilicia Pedias is scanty because the ancient city lies under the modern one, but Jewish/Judaizing inscriptions from Cilicia Tracheia suggest 'the Jewish population of Tarsus and other Cilician cities must have been considerable.' Qualitative scholarly assessment only - Population left blank. Dated to c. 40 CE (Paul's Cilician years c. 37-43 CE), c. Also cites Philo, Legatio 281 (Agrippa I's letter, c. 40 CE) for Jews in Cilicia generally (regional). Later Cilician evidence (menorah coffin from Elaiussa, Mopsuestia building) is late antique and outside the period.

Wilson (Tyndale Bulletin 54.1, 2003): Paul's stay in Tarsus/Cilicia ended when Barnabas went to Tarsus to find him (Acts 11:25); Ramsay dates this to the early months of AD 43 (Hengel & Schwemer allow 3-4 years in Cilicia, Wilson at least 5). Paul, a Jew of Tarsus, resident there c. 37-43 CE; no count.

Acts 21:39 and 22:3 (NRSVUE): Paul says 'I am a Jew from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of an important city' and 'I am a Jew born in Tarsus in Cilicia but brought up in this city [Jerusalem] at the feet of Gamaliel'. Literary attestation of a Jew holding citizenship of Tarsus (implying a Jewish citizen body there, per Ramsay and others). Year = conventional date of Paul's arrest in Jerusalem, c. 57 CE (not given in the text). No count.
